title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework
summary: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.

title: The Bipartible Architecture Pattern: Transparently Directing HTTP Requests over InfiniBand
comment: Presented at 8th International Workshop on Containers and New Orchestration Paradigms for Isolated Environments in HPC
summary:
Large-scale compute (HPC) systems with coherent-memory workloads often deploy InfiniBand (IB) networks for high-bandwidth and low-latency inter-node and storage communication. A separate TCP network is typically used for control-plane and general-purpose communication. The last decade has seen the rise of cloud-native software patterns. These patterns are characterized by container-based software distribution and inter-node and storage communication over TCP/IP. In an unoptimized HPC environment, a cloud-native workload will typically use HTTP for some or all communication.
  This paper introduces the Bipartible architecture pattern to optimize cloud-native workload traffic in HPC environments. This paper focuses on optimizing HTTP storage service requests. These requests are transparently transformed onto IB traffic without modifying workload implementation or network configuration. This is achieved by 'cloning' a global HTTP service (BPService) onto the HPC cluster compute host(s) where the workload executes at scale. Provided the global persistent storage is on the IB network the HTTP service requests are returned to the workload via IB and not TCP/IP.
  The feasibility of this pattern is demonstrated by implementing a prototype BPService for S3 and a Hybrid-BPService (service metadata is accessed over TCP, bulk data over IB) for a software repository service. We offer this pattern in addition to many alternative approaches to address the performance challenges of executing workloads written to cloud-native design patterns in HPC environments. Finally, while the initial results are encuraging signficant validation of any service must be performed under both read and write scenarios before deployment into production is planned.

title: Lower Bounds for the Distributed Computation of Degeneracy and k-Core
summary: The degeneracy of a graph $G$ is the maximum integer $k$ such that $G$ has a non-empty $k$-core, where the $k$-core is the largest induced subgraph with minimum degree $k$. Computing the $k$-core of a graph $G$ is P-complete. In the decentralized setting, the sequential peeling algorithm can be distributed so that the core value of every node, i.e., the largest integer $k$ for which the node belongs to the $k$-core, is computed in $O(n)$ rounds in $n$-node networks, where adjacent nodes exchange only $O(\log n)$ bits at each round, i.e., in the standard CONGEST model. However, while $Ω(D)$ rounds is a trivial lower bound for these problems in networks of diameter $D$, this does not rule out the existence of an algorithm running in $O(D)+o(n)$ rounds in CONGEST, as it is the case for many very important graph problems, including MST. We show that it is unlikely that such an algorithm exists, or, if it does exist, then it requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds. Specifically, our first main result states that, for any $ε>0$, approximating the degeneracy up to a multiplicative factor $2-ε$ requires $\tildeΩ(\sqrt{n})$ rounds in CONGEST even in networks of diameter $O(\log n)$, and still $\tildeΩ(n^{1/3})$ rounds in networks of constant diameter. We also show that improving this lower bound seems challenging, as we demonstrate that the newer frameworks cannot be used as black boxes to obtain a better lower bound for degeneracy. Our second main result provides a better bound, albeit conditional. It states that, unless the well-known circuit value problem (CVP) admits a parallel polynomial speedup -- an outcome considered unlikely -- it holds that, for every $ε>δ>0$, deciding whether a graph is 2-degenerate cannot be solved in $O(D+ n^{1-ε})$ rounds with $O(n^δ)$-time parallel local computation per round at each node.

title: Sustaining In-Network Computation in Satellite Networks: An Architecture for Semantic Continuity
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures. Submitted to IEEE Wireless Communications
summary: Satellite computations often outlast the paths and providers initially serving them. We argue that in-network computing should organize changing execution opportunities around one continuing logical computation: workers execute ready operations, while consumers recognize which results already contribute. We present an architecture separating logical computation, stream context, and physical binding, and show in wildfire assessment how retained observations support recomputation while reachable association history stays in place. A 300-node Linux prototype examines placement, dependency assembly, and continuation. Across 120 images, stage-wise placement delivers 82.08% of positions within deadlines versus 76.06% for single-node placement, while traces separate blocked output delivery from dependencies split across providers. Across 50 observations with 20-node isolation, Confirmation-Coordinated Rebinding (CCR) coordinates replanning, source replay, cross-attempt acceptance, and in-band confirmation to complete all 50 observations with verified outputs using seven replays and 13 ignored duplicate outputs.

title: High-Throughput Serving of Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe with Regime-Aware Megakernels and Kernel Fusion
summary: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR leaderboards. Serving it efficiently takes more than fast operators: continuous batching changes the amount and mix of work at every iteration, and the best fusion granularity changes with it. We present a serving engine that, for every pass, chooses between persistent megakernels and chains of fused kernels at crossovers measured offline. On an H100 SXM GPU, throughput of our accuracy-preserving serving peaks at 4,345x real time, 1.39x the peak of tuned vLLM, and is up to 4.39x faster at low concurrency; on B200 it peaks at 6,367x, 1.64x vLLM at the highest concurrency we measured. Word error rate (WER) is 1.91 to 1.93% against 1.88 to 1.93% for vLLM. Within a 400 ms budget for p95 end-to-end completion time, it serves 8x as many concurrent requests. Choosing per pass beats either level alone: 23% higher throughput than always using megakernels at 128 concurrent requests, and 9% higher than always using fused kernels at 8. Opt-in switches, including greedy MoE layer skipping, add 13 to 16% throughput on B200 for offline jobs that can accept higher WER.
